verdict.root_cause: cartservice cannot reach its Redis backing store and dies during startup initialization, so it never accepts cart RPCs. Its connect attempts name the redis-cart host on port 6380 — not Redis's default 6379 — with the exception thrown from the cart-store initialization path called straight from program startup, producing a restart loop roughly every 1-30 seconds from ~08:50:22 onward [tr_7c90a77b1763]. Because cartservice is unavailable, every checkoutservice PlaceOrder aborts at the GetCart leaf, and that error propagates up through checkoutservice's PlaceOrder span, the frontend gRPC client span and the frontend HTTP root — which is exactly why checkoutservice, frontend and loadgenerator all alerted at 08:50 while checkoutservice itself is internally healthy [tr_8338f7487f5d]. checkoutservice is the caller that noticed, not the fault: it has no changes in the window [tr_a7140baea402], its own error ratio actually fell versus baseline [tr_28c109c65274], its logs carry no error lines and it keeps accepting new orders throughout [tr_0ec22ffb17fe], and its self time is ~0.1ms per span [tr_8338f7487f5d]. The best-supported mechanism is a wrong endpoint value for the cart backing store: the port in the connection configuration does not point at a listening Redis, and requests break because that value is wrong.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent lines converge on cartservice and away from checkoutservice. (1) Traces: all 6 of 6 checkoutservice traces in the window fail fast (1.2-1.6ms) at the same leaf — the call to cart service GetCart from prepareOrderItemsAndShippingQuoteFromCart — with the error inherited upward to the frontend root; no payment span is ever created, and no span is stalled or unclosed [tr_8338f7487f5d]. That both explains the simultaneous checkoutservice/frontend/loadgenerator alerts and rules out checkoutservice-internal latency or exhaustion. (2) checkoutservice's own signals are clean: zero changes recorded [tr_a7140baea402], error ratio ~2.5x below its own baseline with no step change [tr_28c109c65274], and logs containing only info-severity lines with orders still starting steadily through 08:51 [tr_0ec22ffb17fe]. (3) cartservice logs pin the mechanism: healthy, millisecond cart operations at 08:20, then a startup crash loop in which every failure originates in the backing-store connect path called from program main, with no request-handling lines at all afterwards — a crash loop, not slow serving or pool exhaustion [tr_7c90a77b1763]. The distinguishing detail is the endpoint itself: the recorded target is redis-cart:6380, a non-default Redis port. If the value is wrong, the wrongness of the value is what breaks every request — the connect never lands, so this is bad_config and the fix is reverting the endpoint to the correct port rather than restarting a pod that will crash again. Two competing stories were checked and demoted: the 300ms egress delay injected on productcatalogservice was withdrawn at 06:09, about 2.7 hours before onset, and it was a constant offset with zero jitter, so it was not in effect at 08:50 [tr_443caba87a56]; and cartservice's span-derived error-ratio series is absent in both the incident and baseline windows, so that emptiness reflects missing instrumentation rather than a traffic collapse and contributes nothing either way [tr_6c8f032b5bde].
open_questions: No change history was ever queried for cartservice or for the redis-cart deployment, so nothing in this briefing shows who or what set the port to 6380, or when. The bad_config reading rests on 6380 being non-default, not on a recorded edit.
It was not confirmed that redis-cart is actually listening on 6379 (or on any port) right now. If Redis itself is down or was moved, 6380 could be the correct value and the endpoint reading is wrong.

Timeline mismatch: checkoutservice logs show orders ceasing to complete from ~08:47:31 [tr_0ec22ffb17fe], but the cartservice crash loop is only visible from ~08:50:22 [tr_7c90a77b1763] and the traces cluster after 08:50:48 [tr_8338f7487f5d]. What happened in the ~3-minute gap — an earlier, slower cartservice degradation before the crash loop began — is unexplained.

The mixed failure latencies per connect attempt, sub-second to ~30 seconds [tr_7c90a77b1763], are not fully consistent with a pure closed-port rejection and hint at a network-path or DNS component that was not investigated.
No cartservice resource metrics (memory, CPU, connections) or redis-cart-side evidence were collected at all; the four unmeasured edges triage flagged remain unmeasured.
Past incidents were withheld from this briefing, so no corpus comparison informed this verdict.

alternatives.root_cause: The redis-cart backing store itself is down or unreachable (crashed, evicted, or network-isolated), and cartservice's connection configuration is correct — it simply cannot reach a store that no longer exists.
alternatives.why_not: The connect target recorded is port 6380, which is not Redis's default, pointing at the value rather than the peer; and no evidence was gathered from redis-cart itself. Still very much alive as a hypothesis, since nothing confirmed what port redis-cart is actually listening on.

alternatives.root_cause: A cartservice deploy shipped an artifact carrying the wrong backing-store endpoint baked in, so the running version cannot initialize.
alternatives.why_not: No change history was queried for cartservice, so there is no deploy record supporting this; and the failing element is a connection endpoint value, which is configuration rather than a wrong artifact reference. Would be promoted if a cartservice deploy is found at ~08:47-08:50.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no change in observed behaviour should follow from this proposal. cartservice should be expected to continue its startup crash loop (repeated connect-to-redis-cart:6380 failures and unhandled initialization exceptions in the cart-service log stream, restarts every 1-30s) and every checkoutservice PlaceOrder trace should continue to error at the GetCart leaf, until someone runs the two queries named below and then acts. The next observation that matters is not a metric shift but two missing evidence items: (1) a change_history query for cartservice and for the redis-cart deployment, which would show whether a prior configuration exists and whether the port value was edited inside the window; (2) confirmation of what port redis-cart is actually listening on right now.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if change history for cartservice does in fact contain a recorded prior configuration with the cart backing-store port set to 6379 and an edit to 6380 timestamped inside the incident window — in that case revert_config on cartservice meets both of its preconditions and should be proposed immediately, with the expected effect that the cart-service log stream stops emitting connect-failure and initialization-exception lines within ~60s of container recreation, GetCartAsync request lines resume, and checkoutservice traces stop erroring at the GetCart leaf. It is also wrong if the operator's judgement is that a blind restart is worth trying; I judge it is not, because the evidence locates the fault in a configuration value read at startup, and a restart_service that preserves that value would reproduce the identical crash on the next boot, costing an outage extension for no information.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is time: cartservice stays down and checkout stays broken for as long as the two missing queries take. The risk I am refusing to take is larger. revert_config's preconditions are explicitly unmet — no change history was ever queried for cartservice or redis-cart [tr_7c90a77b1763 names 6380 as non-default but records no edit], so there is no known-good prior configuration to restore and 'revert' would be a guess at a value. If redis-cart itself is down or was deliberately moved to 6380, then 6380 is correct, the endpoint reading is wrong, and reverting the port to 6379 would point cartservice at nothing while destroying the evidence of what the value used to be. The ~3-minute unexplained gap between orders ceasing at 08:47:31 [tr_0ec22ffb17fe] and the crash loop appearing at 08:50:22 [tr_7c90a77b1763], plus connect failures ranging from sub-second to ~30 seconds [tr_7c90a77b1763] which do not fit a pure closed-port rejection, both suggest a network-path or DNS component upstream of the port value that a config revert would not touch. restart_service is separately unavailable on its own terms: its precondition is evidence pointing at process state rather than at a change, and this evidence points at a configuration value.
proposal.blast_radius: Nobody sees a change, because nothing changes. For the reader's planning: had revert_config been proposed, its blast radius would be cartservice's container recreate plus a traffic shift onto whichever redis-cart endpoint the reverted value names, and the callers who would notice are checkoutservice (which calls GetCart from prepareOrderItemsAndShippingQuoteFromCart) and, propagating up, frontend's gRPC PlaceOrder client span and frontend's HTTP root, and loadgenerator — the three services that alerted at 08:50 [tr_8338f7487f5d]. Those three remain affected by the ongoing outage during the abstention.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical alerts on checkout and frontend simultaneously with load generator impact indicate a real user-facing failure that cannot be dismissed. The shared checkout dependencies leave the cause open, so no fault class is asserted yet.
